Given the vector cross product condition \vec{a} \times \vec{b} = 2(\vec{a} \times \vec{c})

This implies that \vec{b} - 2\vec{c} is parallel to \vec{a}, so \vec{b} - 2\vec{c} = \lambda \vec{a} for some scalar \lambda
Compute the magnitude squared of \vec{b} - 2\vec{c}:
|\vec{b} - 2\vec{c}|^2 = |\vec{b}|^2 + 4|\vec{c}|^2 - 4(\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c})
Given |\vec{b}| = 4, |\vec{c}| = 2, and angle between \vec{b} and \vec{c} is 60^\circ
\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c} = |\vec{b}| |\vec{c}| \cos 60^\circ = 4 \times 2 \times \frac{1}{2} = 4
Substitute into the squared magnitude: |\vec{b} - 2\vec{c}|^2 = 4^2 + 4(2^2) - 4(4) = 16 + 16 - 16 = 16
Since |\vec{b} - 2\vec{c}| = |\lambda| |\vec{a}| and |\vec{a}| = 1, we have |\lambda| = 4
Since \vec{b} - 2\vec{c} is collinear with \vec{a}, the cross product evaluates to |\vec{a} \times \vec{c}| = 0
→ (A)
